headline: IBM claims world's first sub-1 nanometer chip with 100 billion transistors
summary: The new nanostack architecture packs nearly 100 billion transistors onto a fingernail-sized chip, promising up to 50% higher performance or 70% greater energy efficiency for AI data centers.
details: IBM's new nanostack architecture integrates nearly 100 billion transistors on a chip the size of a human fingernail. This is almost double the density of their previous generation, aiming for a significant leap in compute performance and energy efficiency.

IBM describes this as the "world's first sub-1 nanometer chip technology," specifically the 0.7-nanometer or 7 angstrom node. This terminology refers to performance expectations rather than actual physical feature sizes, which have diverged from node numbers for decades.

To overcome physical scaling limits, the nanostack architecture vertically stacks transistors in a staggered layout. This builds on their previous nanosheet transistors used in the 2-nanometer chip node from 2021.

The basic unit consists of two stacked transistors, each with three 5-nanometer thick nanosheets. Projections indicate this could lead to 50% higher computing performance or 70% greater energy efficiency compared to IBM's 2-nanometer chips.

IBM also showcased a 40% improvement in scaling for static random-access memory (SRAM) using a staggered-channel design. This is crucial for AI workloads that demand high bandwidth and efficiency, addressing a recent slowdown in SRAM scaling.

While IBM researches and develops this technology, it does not manufacture commercial chips. Instead, it partners with semiconductor companies like Rapidus and Samsung to commercialize its innovations.

headline: British Police built crime-prediction machine, but some results couldn't be trusted
summary: Bristol police used machine learning to assign risk scores to nearly half a million people, but two models were abandoned after being deemed untrustworthy by city council staff.
details: The Think Family Database, launched in 2016 by Bristol City Council and Avon and Somerset Police, holds sensitive records on nearly half a million people in Bristol. Officials used machine-learning models to assign risk scores to thousands of adults and children, aiming to create a "picture of threat, harm, and risk." One police data scientist described the process as dumping data into a "big bucket" and stirring it to get a "lovely risk score."

This risk scoring was part of a broader predictive analytics program by Avon and Somerset Police, which included at least 23 separate models. These algorithms aimed to identify risks like committing burglary, failing to appear in court, going missing, or becoming a victim of domestic abuse. The Offender Management App, designed to hold data on around 300,000 people, was described by one senior officer as creating a "league table" of dangerous criminals.

The public was often unaware of how these predictive tools were developed and used. John Pegram, a local police accountability leader, only learned about the Offender Management App years after its creation and suspected he was included. His request for data usage was initially refused, and even after hiring solicitors, police confirmed his inclusion but declined further details.

A joint investigation by WIRED, Liberty Investigates, Bristol Cable, and Lighthouse Reports, based on hundreds of pages of public records, revealed critical issues. At least two risk-scoring models were quietly abandoned after Bristol City Council staff deemed them untrustworthy. Documents show government inspectors and independent reviewers highlighted a "startling lack of transparency" and warned of undermined public trust.

Police data, comprising over 36,000 model performance scores, showed "genuinely poor predictive performance" in some cases, according to an independent analyst. These findings emerge as the UK plans to expand predictive analytics and AI in its criminal justice system. The former chief constable of Avon and Somerset, Andy Marsh, now heads the national standard-setting body and advocates for "injecting AI like heroin" into police work.
